title: What Does It Really Mean To Program With AI: A Conversation with Joy Ebertz
gist: A podcast between architect Michael Stiefel and Joy Ebertz on what programming with AI means: AI works better on constrained code, tests and unambiguous requirements become the gating factor as code review fades, and 'code written by AI' ranges from vibe-coded internal tools to carefully validated pair programming. Both worry the industry has no way to train junior engineers now that AI does their learning tasks.

insights.claim: An architect's distinctive value is long-term thinking: pulling in where the company is going next and how other teams' work fits, since technically perfect systems are worthless if the business does not survive.
insights.speaker: Joy Ebertz
insights.so_what: Long-horizon technical choices are where architects protect business survival, which affects execution risk in tech companies.
insights.quote: you could build something absolutely technically perfect that's going to last a hundred billion customers, whatever, but if your business doesn't survive to next month, it doesn't matter.
insights.locator: Michael Stiefel: Right. I think that's a valid point.

insights.claim: Architects must translate in both directions, explaining business goals to technical people and technical goals to business people (Gregor Hohpe's 'elevator architect').
insights.speaker: Michael Stiefel
insights.so_what: Translation skill is increasingly the scarce capability as AI handles implementation.
insights.quote: you have to be able to talk to the technical people and explain to them the business goals
insights.locator: Right. I think that's a valid point.

insights.claim: Large monolith-to-microservice splits rarely finish; Ebertz says success is typically about 75% completion, and architects struggle with long-horizon projects that are hard to prioritize and give little feedback.
insights.speaker: Joy Ebertz
insights.so_what: Expect partial migrations and long timelines when assessing re-architecture claims.
insights.quote: you don't actually expect it to finish. You expect it to get about 75% of the way there
insights.locator: What about architecture do you hate?

insights.claim: AI performs better when constrained to a smaller code base and problem, like humans, which argues for microservices, yet Ebertz's team merged three drifting JavaScript services into one repo so AI could spread good practices between them.
insights.speaker: Joy Ebertz
insights.so_what: No settled answer on whether AI favors monoliths or microservices; architecture choices remain case-specific.
insights.quote: if you can constrain the code base, they're going to do better.
insights.locator: Yes, that's an interesting point.

insights.claim: Regenerating a whole service from scratch on each bug report is plausible because AI builds much faster, but requires use cases fully defined in tests, which is a limiting factor for many teams.
insights.speaker: Joy Ebertz
insights.so_what: Test coverage and requirement completeness gate whether regenerative development is viable.
insights.quote: I do think the thing we're missing is good testing.
insights.locator: I haven't actually dabbled in anything that extreme.

insights.claim: Because AI can regenerate large chunks of code, teams must now document what systems are supposed to do, something the industry has been lazy about, whereas previously old systems were left untouched because nobody remembered the requirements.
insights.speaker: Joy Ebertz
insights.so_what: Documentation and requirement capture become a precondition for AI-driven modernization of legacy systems.
insights.quote: you need to know what it's supposed to do and you need to somehow document that
insights.locator: Yes, it's interesting because I guess

themes.theme: Requirements, tests and code review as bottlenecks

insights.claim: AI coding agents may game tests: one fixes broken tests by rewriting them or deleting them, so Ebertz's team added instructions to agent files such as 'Don't just delete tests'.
insights.speaker: Joy Ebertz
insights.so_what: Agent-written tests need separation from agent-written code; guardrails belong in agent configuration.
insights.quote: I'll delete the test
insights.locator: Yes, exactly. And I also have had cases

insights.claim: Tests become more important in AI-driven development, and the gating factor may be unambiguous requirements and the ability to feed field feedback back into them, not AI slop.
insights.speaker: Michael Stiefel
insights.so_what: The constraint on AI delivery shifts from coding speed to specification quality.
insights.quote: This might actually turn out to be the gating factor.
insights.locator: This might actually turn out to be the gating factor.

insights.claim: Code review is currently gating AI-generated output but is an artificial gate; reviewers overwhelmed by volume get sloppy, so it will be replaced by tests and requirements.
insights.speaker: Joy Ebertz
insights.so_what: Predicts a shift in engineering spend from review labor to test and spec tooling.
insights.quote: So I think they have to go away and we have to find a way for them to go away.
insights.locator: I think that's right because I've been hearing recently

insights.claim: Ebertz asks the AI 'what assumptions have you made?' after it produces a plan and sometimes finds huge wrong assumptions; planning before coding is her default workflow.
insights.speaker: Joy Ebertz
insights.so_what: A cheap practice to catch hidden assumptions before AI writes code.
insights.quote: My favorite question to ask it when it finishes the plan is what assumptions have you made?
insights.locator: Yes. We usually do a plan first and then have it code.

insights.claim: Constraints and explicit recognition of assumptions are the critical concepts for future developers because AI flexibility removes natural limits; unclear constraints cause circular planning meetings.
insights.speaker: Michael Stiefel
insights.so_what: Problem definition skill gains value as implementation gets cheap.
insights.quote: constraints always help you
insights.locator: Does this flexibility that AI gives you become a nightmare?

insights.claim: A reported statement at Google Next that 75% of Google code is written by AI is ambiguous, since it may include configuration and tooling, and about 80% of system code may be non-core such as error checking and input handling; Stiefel could not verify it.
insights.speaker: Michael Stiefel
insights.so_what: Treat 'percent of code written by AI' metrics skeptically unless the definition is clear.
insights.quote: 75% of the code written at Google is written by AI in one way or another
insights.locator: Really Mean? [32:06]

insights.claim: AI coding spans two modes: fully vibe coding for imperfect internal tools, and carefully specified, validated work on essential backend systems, effectively pair programming with AI.
insights.speaker: Joy Ebertz
insights.so_what: Adoption statistics mix very different risk levels; critical systems still require human validation.
insights.quote: I am a hundred percent vibe coding.
insights.locator: I'm curious now too, because if you had asked me

insights.claim: Humans remain most important where performance, security and end-to-end user experience matter, and AI struggles with large complex problems such as sprawling authorization rules and even simple tasks like centering on a screen.
insights.speaker: Joy Ebertz
insights.so_what: AI coding leaves durable demand for specialists in security, performance and complex domains.
insights.quote: You're naming all of the places where I think humans are still the most important.
insights.locator: You're naming all of the places where I think humans are still the most important.

insights.claim: Authorization starts simple and accretes rules into an incomprehensible monolith; the best path is breaking it into constrained domains, after which AI could handle it, though Ebertz would be cautious about letting AI do the breakup.
insights.speaker: Joy Ebertz
insights.so_what: Constrained domain decomposition is a precondition for effective AI assistance on legacy systems.
insights.quote: I think part of why people struggle with authorization is it starts simple.
insights.locator: I think part of why people struggle with authorization is it starts simple.

insights.claim: It is uncertain whether AI can orchestrate microservices in the middle tier; it may work for constrained business problems, but as complexity grows teams may cross a chasm where neither AI nor people can orchestrate.
insights.speaker: Joy Ebertz
insights.so_what: Raises risk of unmaintainable AI-generated systems as they scale.
insights.quote: It certainly seems plausible that we could get there.
insights.locator: It certainly seems plausible that we could get there.

insights.claim: Industry has not figured out how to train junior engineers because AI now does the tasks on which juniors learned; juniors give AI generic instructions and get spaghetti code while seniors embed architecture in prompts.
insights.speaker: Joy Ebertz
insights.so_what: Talent pipeline risk for software firms; seniors may become scarce and expensive over time.
insights.quote: we're not teaching them to use the AI effectively, but we're also not teaching them how to do it without the AI
insights.locator: I think it's related to that, but one of the things I worry about

insights.claim: Most companies are not hiring junior engineers, which Ebertz calls shortsighted since senior staff will retire; some firms hire juniors only because they are cheaper than tokens, which may not last.
insights.speaker: Joy Ebertz
insights.so_what: Hiring freezes on juniors may create a future senior shortage, and token costs influence hiring.
insights.quote: Most companies at the moment are just not hiring junior engineers too, which also feels shortsighted.
insights.locator: Yes. I honestly don't know if I would tell somebody to go into CS today.

insights.claim: Faster AI-driven change risks the rapid loss of low-level knowledge, such as debugging problems from compiler switches, that Stiefel resolved only because he remembered earlier eras.
insights.speaker: Michael Stiefel
insights.so_what: Abstraction layers piling up reduces human capability to debug deep failures.
insights.quote: My fear is if we go so fast, this old knowledge will be rapidly forgotten.
insights.locator: So my fear is in this transition period

insights.claim: Companies are weakly incentivized to train juniors under capitalism, and people usually act only after a crash or failure.
insights.speaker: Michael Stiefel
insights.so_what: Training shortfalls may only be corrected after a visible failure.
insights.quote: all you need is one bad situation and everybody will now panic in the opposite direction.
insights.locator: Well, I mean, I think we will see evidence of this quickly
